Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Model
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Margaret still remembers the weight of the steering wheel in her hands, the way the afternoon sun cut through the windshield at just the wrong angle. She was sixty-three then, still working steadily as a model, driving home from a shoot in the city. The intersection was familiar—she’d taken it hundreds of times. But that day, a man on a bicycle appeared from her blind spot as she turned right. She didn’t see him until she felt the thud, the terrible give of metal against flesh. She stopped the car immediately, got out, and found him lying on the pavement, his leg bent at an angle that made her stomach turn. She called 911, knelt beside him, and held his hand until the ambulance came. But in the weeks that followed, that single image—his face twisted in pain, his leg, the blood—began to replay in her mind, not as a memory she could set aside, but as a loop she could not stop.

Margaret is sixty-six now, widowed for eight years, and still modeling part-time, mostly for high-end catalogues and the occasional editorial. She has always taken pride in her composure, her ability to hold a pose for hours, to project calm and confidence. But since the accident, that composure has eroded from the inside. She cannot relax, even when she knows she is in a safe place. At home, in her quiet apartment, she finds herself sitting on the edge of the sofa, her shoulders hunched, her hands gripping her knees. Her body feels constantly tense, as if it is waiting for something terrible to happen. She has trouble concentrating during fittings and shoots; she forgets instructions, loses her place in the sequence of poses, and has to ask photographers to repeat themselves. They have been patient, but she sees the flicker of irritation in their eyes, and it deepens her sense of humiliation.

What frightens Margaret most is not the memory of the accident itself, but what she has come to believe about herself because of it. She is certain that somebody else—someone more alert, more capable—would not have gotten into this situation. She replays the turn again and again, imagining how another driver would have checked the blind spot twice, would have slowed down, would have seen the cyclist in time. She feels permanently humiliated by what happened, as though the accident has stained her character, made her visibly incompetent to anyone who knows. And beneath that is a sharper, more private pain: she will never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. She knows, rationally, that she could not have undone the accident once it began, but the thought sits in her chest like a stone. She should have done something—screamed, swerved, braked harder—and she did not.

The avoidance crept in slowly, over weeks and months. She stopped driving through that intersection, then stopped driving on that side of town entirely. She began to take back roads, then to ask friends for rides, then to cancel appointments altogether if she could not arrange transportation. Her agent noticed. She lost two catalogue jobs because she could not get to the studio on time. She told herself she was being careful, but she knew, deep down, that she was shrinking her life. Even walking near traffic became difficult; she would flinch at the sound of a bicycle bell, her heart hammering, her body bracing for a crash that had already happened.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a shoot last month. The photographer asked her to stand near an open window for natural light. She could not do it. She felt her throat close, her palms sweat, and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she stood trembling for ten minutes. She could not explain why. She could not tell him that the window reminded her of the moment she saw the cyclist’s face, that the light was the same, that she felt the shame rising again like a wave. She went home that evening and made an appointment with a therapist. She is afraid that she will never feel like herself again, that the accident has rewritten who she is. But she is also hoping—cautiously, quietly—that someone can help her find a way to live with what she has done.
